## Represent objects numerically

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- [Scalar]{.alert} $a$ — one quantity
  - `a = np.float64(22.5)`
  - temperature
  - price
  - scale factor

- [Vector]{.alert} $\vct{x}$ — several related quantities
  - `x = np.array([3, 2])`
  - coordinates
  - pixel values
  - node scores
  - system state
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- [Matrix]{.alert} $\mat{A}$ — rectangular arrangement of quantities
  - `A = np.array([[1, .5], [0, 1]])`
  - data table or image
  - relationships or constraints
  - action on vectors

- [Tensor]{.alert} $\tens{T}$ — quantities indexed in several directions
  - `T = np.zeros((32, 32, 3))`
  - color image
  - batch of matrices
  - sequence of network states
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Numerical representations are models of objects that allow us to compute with them.
:::

## Act on these objects via transformations to obtain new objects

::: {.diagram-flow}
<div class="diagram-node">input object(s) or state(s)<br>$\vct{x}$<br>$\mat{X}$</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow">→</div>
<div class="diagram-node">action or relationships<br>$\mat{A}$</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow">→</div>
<div class="diagram-node">output object(s) or state(s)<br>$\vct{y}=\mat{A}\vct{x}$<br>$\mat{Y}=\mat{A}\mat{X}$</div>
:::

### Examples of actions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- rotate or reflect
- stretch, scale, or compress
- shear
- project onto a lower-dimensional space
- change coordinate systems
- permute or select coordinates
- transform object coordinates to camera coordinates
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- mix colors or features
- smooth, sharpen, or filter an image
- reduce dimension or extract features
- update a network state
- apply a Markov-chain transition
- average or combine measurements
:::
:::

## Images contain important patterns

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
<svg class="diagram-image" viewBox="0 0 500 300" width="78%" role="img" aria-label="Synthetic landscape made from smooth bands"><defs><linearGradient id="image-sky" y2="1"><stop stop-color="#ecf7fc"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#78b8dc"/></linearGradient><linearGradient id="image-land" x2="1"><stop stop-color="#203d2e"/><stop offset=".5" stop-color="#75a35e"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#294a36"/></linearGradient></defs><rect x="20" y="15" width="460" height="270" rx="8" fill="url(#image-sky)"/><circle cx="365" cy="80" r="40" fill="#ffe39a"/><path d="M20 220Q120 140 230 215T480 165V285H20Z" fill="url(#image-land)"/><path d="M20 255Q120 215 240 260T480 225V285H20Z" fill="#183345" opacity=".8"/></svg>
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
Each color channel is a matrix

$$\mat{M}=(m_{jk})_{j=1,k=1}^{m,n}$$

Once an image has been represented as a matrix, linear algebra can reveal important patterns.

[Singular value decomposition (SVD)]{.alert} decomposes a matrix into patterns ordered by their contribution.
:::
:::

<div class="component-row">
<div><div class="component-image component-sky" role="img" aria-label="Simple vertical brightness component"></div><span class="diagram-label">simple pattern</span></div>
<span class="diagram-arrow">+</span>
<div><div class="component-image component-land" role="img" aria-label="Simple landscape component"></div><span class="diagram-label">simple pattern</span></div>
<span class="diagram-arrow">+ ···</span>
</div>

Keep the most important patterns for compression, denoising, or discovering structure

## Represent data for regression

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 620 390" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Scatterplot of five observations and a regression line"><path d="M55 330H585M55 330V25" stroke="#555" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M80 315L555 55" stroke="#f39c34" stroke-width="6"/><g fill="#007acc"><circle cx="110" cy="285" r="11"/><circle cx="205" cy="245" r="11"/><circle cx="300" cy="205" r="11"/><circle cx="405" cy="125" r="11"/><circle cx="520" cy="80" r="11"/></g><g font-size="30" fill="#333"><text x="565" y="315">𝑥</text><text x="70" y="45">𝑦</text></g></svg>

::: {.diagram-label}
observed pairs $(x_i,y_i)$
:::

::: {.vspace}
Linear model

$$y_i\approx c_0+c_1x_i$$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
One equation per observation

\begin{align*}
c_0+c_1x_1&\approx y_1\\
c_0+c_1x_2&\approx y_2\\
&\ \vdots\\
c_0+c_1x_n&\approx y_n
\end{align*}

The same system

$$
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}
1&x_1\\
1&x_2\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
1&x_n
\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\vct{c}=\begin{bmatrix}c_0\\c_1\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\vct{b}=\begin{bmatrix}y_1\\y_2\\\vdots\\y_n\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$\mat{A}\vct{c}\approx\vct{b}$$
:::
:::

## Represent a network by an incidence matrix

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 520 390" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Three-node directed network"><defs><marker id="incidence-arrowhead" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="9" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0,10 3.5,0 7" fill="#7895a8"/></marker></defs><g stroke="#7895a8" stroke-width="6" fill="none" marker-end="url(#incidence-arrowhead)"><path d="M145 105L365 105"/><path d="M382 137L287 287"/><path d="M138 137L238 283"/></g><g fill="#f8fbfd" stroke="#007acc" stroke-width="6"><circle cx="110" cy="105" r="42"/><circle cx="410" cy="105" r="42"/><circle cx="260" cy="325" r="42"/></g><g font-size="32" text-anchor="middle"><text x="110" y="116">1</text><text x="410" y="116">2</text><text x="260" y="336">3</text></g><g font-size="25"><text x="250" y="85">e₁</text><text x="352" y="235">e₂</text><text x="155" y="235">e₃</text></g></svg>
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
Oriented edges

$$e_1:1\to2,\qquad e_2:2\to3,\qquad e_3:1\to3$$

Node–edge incidence matrix

$$
\mat{B}=
\begin{bmatrix}
-1& 0&-1\\
 1&-1& 0\\
 0& 1& 1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

$\mat{B}$ represents the network structure.

- one row per node
- one column per edge
- $-1$ at the tail; $+1$ at the head
:::
:::

## A matrix is an action—predict before multiplying {#a-matrix-is-an-action-predict-before-multiplying}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 520 390" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Vector x rotated counterclockwise to R x"><defs><marker id="rotation-arrowhead-blue" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="9" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0,10 3.5,0 7" fill="#007acc"/></marker><marker id="rotation-arrowhead-orange" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="9" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0,10 3.5,0 7" fill="#f39c34"/></marker></defs><path d="M35 300H485M260 365V25" stroke="#777" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M260 300L410 225" stroke="#007acc" stroke-width="8" marker-end="url(#rotation-arrowhead-blue)"/><path d="M260 300L185 150" stroke="#f39c34" stroke-width="8" marker-end="url(#rotation-arrowhead-orange)"/><path d="M333 264A82 82 0 0 0 224 227" fill="none" stroke="#7895a8" stroke-width="5" stroke-dasharray="8 6" marker-end="url(#rotation-arrowhead-orange)"/><foreignObject x="400" y="185" width="90" height="55"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="diagram-label">$\vct{x}$</div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="115" y="105" width="130" height="55"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="diagram-label">$\mat{R}\vct{x}$</div></foreignObject></svg>
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
$$
\mat{R}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\vct{x}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$\vct{x}\longmapsto\mat{R}\vct{x}$$

::: {.exitem}
::: {.exbullet}
$\exstar$
:::
::: {.extext}
Before multiplying

- What geometric action does $\mat{R}$ perform?
- Where does $\vct{x}$ land?
- Then calculate $\mat{R}\vct{x}$

:::
:::
:::
:::

## Composition is multiplication

::: {.diagram-flow}
<div class="diagram-node">object coordinates<br>$\vct{x}_{\text{object}}$</div><div class="diagram-arrow">$\xrightarrow{\mat{A}}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node">world coordinates<br>$\vct{x}_{\text{world}}$</div><div class="diagram-arrow">$\xrightarrow{\mat{B}}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node">camera coordinates<br>$\vct{x}_{\text{camera}}$</div><div class="diagram-arrow">$\xrightarrow{\mat{C}}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node">screen coordinates<br>$\vct{x}_{\text{screen}}$</div>
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="13%"}
:::
::: {.column width="20%" align="center"}
place and orient the object in the world
:::
::: {.column width="7%"}
:::
::: {.column width="20%" align="center"}
express the world relative to the camera
:::
::: {.column width="7%"}
:::
::: {.column width="20%" align="center"}
project camera coordinates onto the screen
:::
::: {.column width="13%"}
:::
:::

One composed action

$$
\vct{x}_{\text{screen}}
=\mat{C}\mat{B}\mat{A}\vct{x}_{\text{object}}
$$

::: {.key-point}
[Order]{.alert} of $\left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{transformations}\\[-0.15em]\text{multiplication}\end{array}\right\}$ matters
:::


## What does the system tell us?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 520 300" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Three constraint lines meeting at the point 3 comma 3"><path d="M40 260H490M40 260V20" stroke="#555" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M40 55L460 245" stroke="#007acc" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M90 260L390 54" stroke="#f39c34" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M250 20V260" stroke="#0f8b8d" stroke-width="5"/><circle cx="250" cy="150" r="10" fill="#c62828"/><text x="267" y="143" font-size="24">(3,3)</text></svg>
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
Three sensors; unknown location $(x,y)$

\begin{align*}
x+y&=6 &&\text{sensor 1}\\
2x-y&=3 &&\text{sensor 2}\\
3x&=9 &&\text{sensor 3}
\end{align*}

All three constraints agree

Third equation is [redundant]{.alert}: sum of the first two

More equations $\ne$ more information
:::
:::

::: {.question-grid}
<div><span class="diagram-label">existence</span><br>Does any solution satisfy every constraint?</div>
<div><span class="diagram-label">uniqueness</span><br>Is there exactly one solution?</div>
<div><span class="diagram-label">information</span><br>Which constraints add something new?</div>
<div><span class="diagram-label">reversibility</span><br>Can outputs determine the inputs?</div>
:::

::: {.key-point}
Solving means understanding the information in a system—not only finding numbers.
:::

## When the constraints cannot all be satisfied

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 620 380" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Scatterplot with a fitted line and residuals"><path d="M55 325H585M55 325V25" stroke="#555" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M80 295L550 70" stroke="#f39c34" stroke-width="6"/><g fill="#007acc"><circle cx="110" cy="285" r="10"/><circle cx="180" cy="220" r="10"/><circle cx="255" cy="235" r="10"/><circle cx="330" cy="160" r="10"/><circle cx="405" cy="155" r="10"/><circle cx="500" cy="85" r="10"/></g><g stroke="#777" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="7 6"><path d="M180 220V247M255 235V211M330 160V175M405 155V139"/></g></svg>

No line passes through every point

So $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ has no exact solution
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1000 430" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Data vector projected onto the plane of possible outputs"><defs><marker id="projection-arrowhead" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="9" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0,10 3.5,0 7" fill="#007acc"/></marker><marker id="projection-arrowhead-orange" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="9" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0,10 3.5,0 7" fill="#f39c34"/></marker></defs><path d="M90 300L650 300L910 395L350 395Z" fill="#dceef7" stroke="#8ba8ba" stroke-width="5"/><path d="M300 350L600 80" stroke="#007acc" stroke-width="8" marker-end="url(#projection-arrowhead)"/><path d="M300 350L600 340" stroke="#f39c34" stroke-width="8" marker-end="url(#projection-arrowhead-orange)"/><path d="M600 340L600 80" stroke="#c62828" stroke-width="6" stroke-dasharray="10 8"/><path d="M575 340H600V315" fill="none" stroke="#333" stroke-width="4"/><circle cx="300" cy="350" r="7" fill="#333"/><text x="270" y="378" font-size="28">0</text><text x="625" y="80" font-size="30">data vector b</text><foreignObject x="365" y="292" width="180" height="55"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="diagram-label">$\mA\hvx$</div></foreignObject><text x="620" y="215" font-size="28">residual</text><text x="665" y="380" font-size="29">all possible outputs A x</text></svg>

$$
\hvx
=\argmin_{\vct{x}}\;\lVert\vct{b}-\mat{A}\vct{x}\rVert^2
$$
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Least squares asks for the closest possible output; projection identifies it geometrically.
:::

## Repeated action reveals a persistent pattern

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 620 390" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Five-node directed web network"><defs><marker id="network-arrowhead" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="7" refX="8" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0,9 3.5,0 7" fill="#7895a8"/></marker></defs><g stroke="#7895a8" stroke-width="5" fill="none" marker-end="url(#network-arrowhead)"><path d="M105 100L270 170M110 285L270 210M510 90L350 170M510 300L350 220M290 170L150 110M330 170L475 100M320 225L480 285M480 285L130 285"/></g><g fill="#f8fbfd" stroke="#007acc" stroke-width="6"><circle cx="90" cy="90" r="40"/><circle cx="90" cy="300" r="40"/><circle cx="310" cy="195" r="60" fill="#d9effb"/><circle cx="530" cy="75" r="40"/><circle cx="530" cy="315" r="40"/></g><g font-size="32" text-anchor="middle"><text x="90" y="101">A</text><text x="90" y="311">B</text><text x="310" y="206">C</text><text x="530" y="86">D</text><text x="530" y="326">E</text></g></svg>
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
A page is important if important pages link to it

A different matrix—built from the network's links—redistributes the node scores.

$$
\vct{p}_{k+1}=\mat{A}\vct{p}_k
$$

Repeated redistribution may approach a steady ranking

$$\mat{A}\vct{p}=\vct{p}$$

[Eigenvectors]{.alert} identify directions that a matrix action preserves
:::
:::

## Where machine learning fits

::: {.diagram-flow}
<div class="diagram-node">one example<br>$\vct{x}$</div><div class="diagram-arrow">→</div>
<div class="diagram-node">$\mat{W}\vct{x}+\vct{b}$<br><span class="small">learned affine layer</span></div><div class="diagram-arrow">→</div>
<div class="diagram-node">nonlinearity</div><div class="diagram-arrow">→</div>
<div class="diagram-node">prediction</div>
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- $\vct{x}$ — input features
  - pixels, measurements, coordinates
- $\mat{W}$ — learned transformation
  - selects and mixes features
- $\vct{b}$ — learned offset
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- nonlinearity — activation
  - ReLU (hockey stick), sigmoid
- prediction — model output
  - class, score, estimated value
:::
:::

Linear algebra supplies representations, transformations, geometry, and scalable operations

Machine learning also needs probability, optimization, nonlinear models, data, and judgment

## Too little information, many answers

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 560 390" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Several vectors ending on the line x one plus x two equals four"><defs><marker id="illposed-arrowhead" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="7" refX="9" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0,10 3.5,0 7" fill="#007acc"/></marker></defs><path d="M55 330H520M55 330V25" stroke="#555" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M75 65L475 325" stroke="#7895a8" stroke-width="6"/><g stroke="#007acc" stroke-width="7" marker-end="url(#illposed-arrowhead)"><path d="M55 330L155 117"/><path d="M55 330L255 182"/><path d="M55 330L355 247"/><path d="M55 330L455 312"/></g><g fill="#f39c34"><circle cx="155" cy="117" r="8"/><circle cx="255" cy="182" r="8"/><circle cx="355" cy="247" r="8"/><circle cx="455" cy="312" r="8"/></g><text x="300" y="105" font-size="27">same measurement</text><text x="280" y="372" font-size="25" text-anchor="middle">many possible vectors</text></svg>
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
One measurement

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1&1\end{bmatrix}\vct{x}=4
$$

Many solutions

$$
\vct{x}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\4\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}1\\3\end{bmatrix},
\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix},\ldots
$$

- existence: yes
- uniqueness: no
- information: insufficient
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
An [ill-posed problem]{.alert} does not determine a unique, stable answer. Here uniqueness fails.
:::

One remedy: add a selection rule—e.g., the [smallest-norm]{.alert}
solution: $\displaystyle\vct{x}_\star
=\argmin_{[\,1\;1\,]\vct{x}=4}\lVert\vct{x}\rVert_2
=\begin{bmatrix}2\\2\end{bmatrix}$

## Almost parallel, almost unknowable

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 620 380" width="100%" role="img" aria-label="Two nearly parallel constraints whose intersection moves far after a small perturbation"><text x="310" y="28" font-size="24" text-anchor="middle">small perturbation</text><path d="M170 58H225" stroke="#f39c34" stroke-width="5"/><text x="238" y="66" font-size="23">original</text><path d="M360 58H415" stroke="#0f8b8d" stroke-width="5" stroke-dasharray="10 8"/><text x="428" y="66" font-size="23">perturbed</text><g stroke-width="5" fill="none"><path d="M40 320L580 104" stroke="#007acc"/><path d="M40 301L580 107" stroke="#f39c34"/><path d="M40 317L580 123" stroke="#0f8b8d" stroke-dasharray="10 8"/></g><path d="M350 190V206" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M342 190H358M342 206H358" stroke="#333" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M120 290L507 133" stroke="#777" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/><circle cx="507" cy="133" r="10" fill="#c62828"/><circle cx="114" cy="290" r="10" fill="#7b1fa2"/><text x="250" y="275" font-size="24">intersection moves far</text></svg>
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
Each system has a unique solution

Nearly parallel constraints make that solution highly sensitive to the data

This is [ill-conditioning]{.alert}
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
A tiny change in the data can cause a large change in the solution.
:::

## Equivalent mathematics, unequal computations

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Mathematically equivalent

$$
\sqrt{1+x^2}-1
=
\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}+1}
$$

For very small $x>0$, direct subtraction combines nearly equal numbers

[Catastrophic cancellation]{.alert} can discard significant digits
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Python double precision:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import numpy as np

x = 1.23456789 * np.array([1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8])  # Edit, then render

direct = np.sqrt(1 + x**2) - 1
rationalized = x**2 / (np.sqrt(1 + x**2) + 1)

print("| $x$ | direct | rationalized |")
print("|---:|---:|---:|")
for x_i, direct_i, rationalized_i in zip(x, direct, rationalized):
    print(f"| ${x_i:.4E}$ | ${direct_i:.4E}$ | ${rationalized_i:.4E}$ |")
```

The rationalized form avoids the subtraction
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Numerical [instability]{.alert} is avoidable error introduced or amplified by the computational method.
:::

## A correct computation can still cost too much

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
### Solving  $\mA \vx = \vb$ for $\vx$

For a dense $n\times n$ matrix, $\mA$

- storage: about $n^2$ numbers
- direct solve: about $n^3$ operations

Double $n$ implies

- $4\times$ the storage
- $8\times$ the arithmetic


:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
1. Use reliable numerical linear algebra packages

    - tested, numerically stable algorithms
    - optimized libraries and available hardware
    - specialized sparse and structured methods

2. Choose the efficient algorithm,
  e.g. `x=np.linalg.solve(A,b)`, not `x=np.linalg.inv(A)@b`

:::
:::

May reduce storage and operations by exploiting [structure]{.alert}: sparsity, symmetry, low rank, …

---

### Compute only what the problem requires

Unnecessary computation

- wastes time
- uses memory and energy
- creates additional opportunities for round-off error to accumulate or propagate

Examples:

- solve $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ directly instead of computing $\mat{A}^{-1}\vct{b}$
- reuse elimination structure or a factorization when many right-hand sides share $\mat{A}$
- exploit sparsity, symmetry, low rank, and other structure

::: {.key-point}
Do no unnecessary computation; for production work, use a tested numerical library
:::

Reliable software cannot fix ill-posedness or remove sensitivity inherent in an ill-conditioned problem.

## Can we trust the answer?

::: {.question-grid}
<div><span class="diagram-label">model / formulation</span><br>Does the mathematical problem determine an appropriate answer?</div>
<div><span class="diagram-label">conditioning</span><br>How much can the answer change when the data change slightly?</div>
<div><span class="diagram-label">algorithm</span><br>Does the computation introduce substantially more error?</div>
<div><span class="diagram-label">cost</span><br>Does the method use the size and structure of the problem efficiently?</div>
<div><span class="diagram-label">verification</span><br>Can residuals, another method, or known structure check the result?</div>
:::

::: {.key-point}
Distinguish an [ill-posed formulation]{.alert}, an [ill-conditioned problem]{.alert}, an [unstable algorithm]{.alert}, and [excessive computational cost]{.alert}.
:::

## Questions we will learn to answer

- How can we represent complicated objects and data?
- When does a system have one solution, many solutions, or none?
- Which information is genuinely new, and which is redundant?
- When can a transformation be reversed?
- How do we find the best approximate answer?
- Which patterns matter most?
